parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: Outside the museum entrance, where you can see the front of the building.

paras.t: This is the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, one of the largest museums in Greece, and often called the best in the world for Minoan art. It holds the great majority of the finds from the palace at Knossos and other Minoan sites on Crete.

The collection covers 5,500 years of Cretan history, from the Neolithic to Roman times. It began in 1883 as a simple collection of antiquities, just as the Minoans were being rediscovered. Crete was then largely self-governing, and that helped keep its finds here, on the island.
If your time is short, look for three highlights first: the Phaistos Disc, the Snake Goddess figures, and the Bull-Leaping Fresco.

The building is worth a glance too. It's a modernist design by the architect Patroklos Karantinos, hired in 1935, and it came through the bombing of the German invasion in 1941. Look for the multicolored veined marble in the building. It echoes the painted imitation marble on Minoan palace walls.

parts.name: The Phaistos Disc
parts.stand: In front of the glass case with the round clay disc.

paras.t: This small clay disc is the Phaistos Disc. It's about 16 centimeters across, with a spiral of signs on each side, in a script and a language nobody knows.

The Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found it in 1908, in the palace of Phaistos near the south coast. Look closely. There are 242 signs in all, of 45 different kinds, and each one was pressed into the soft clay with its own stamp before firing. That's why it's sometimes called an early example of printing with movable type.
Can anyone read it? Many have tried. Scholars think a real decipherment is unlikely unless more examples of these signs turn up somewhere else.

Because it's so unusual, some scholars once suspected a forgery. Archaeologists now generally accept it as genuine. Even its date is uncertain: one scholar puts it between 1850 and 1600 BC, another after 1400 BC.

parts.name: The snake goddesses
parts.stand: At the case with the small faience figures holding up snakes.

paras.t: These figures came from the palace at Knossos, found in 1903, and they date to around 1600 BC. Arthur Evans called the larger one a Snake Goddess and the smaller one a Snake Priestess. Was he right? Scholars still argue.

They're made of faience, a crushed quartz paste that fires to a bright, glassy finish. Now look carefully, because a lot of what you see was restored. The larger figure was missing everything below the waist, and more. The smaller one had no head; Evans and one of his restorers made the head you see today.
Some scholars go further and argue they aren't really holding snakes at all, or at least not as many as Evans thought.
They caused such a stir that forgers got busy. A figure the Boston Museum of Fine Arts bought in 1914, and another in the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore, are now regarded as fakes.

parts.name: The frescoes
parts.stand: Among the frescoes, in front of the panel of the leaping bull.

paras.t: Here is the Bull-Leaping Fresco from Knossos, one of the museum's highlights. Three figures and a bull, drawn with its legs stretched out as if at full gallop. A young man is over the bull's back.

By the accepted convention of Minoan art, women are painted pale and men dark. So by that convention, the figures are read as two women, one at each end, and a young man on the bull. The woman in front holds the horns. And remember, this is the most completely restored of several panels. There are more fragments than made it into this famous reconstruction.
What exactly were they doing, and why? Nobody knows for sure. A century after the discovery, the technique and the reasons remain obscure.
In the fresco rooms nearby, look for the one nicknamed La Parisienne. A French art historian thought she looked like the Parisian women of the day, and the name stuck.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: On your way out, wherever you can pause for a moment.

paras.t: The museum's story runs on into Greek and Roman sculpture. And Crete appears in the Bible too. Acts chapter 27, in the King James Version, tells of the voyage of the apostle Paul. It says they "sailed under Crete, over against Salmone," and "came unto a place which is called The fair havens." There, with sailing now dangerous, Paul admonished them.
Think about what you've seen. They left writing we still can't read. What they left us is bulls, figures with snakes, and one clay disc. And somehow, standing here, they don't feel like strangers.
